edges.effect_quant: This is one of the cleaner geriatric antidepressant safety signals. In a 2026 multi-institutional cohort, SSRI initiation was associated with higher hyponatremia risk than other antidepressant classes overall (HR 1.18, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.38) and especially in adults aged 60 and older (HR 1.29, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.57). In the Stockholm Sodium Cohort of 234,217 first-time SSRI or venlafaxine users, the adjusted odds ratio for profound hyponatremia was 4.29 in the first 3 months and 10.06 in the first 2 weeks after initiation, with older women at highest absolute risk.
edges.population: older adults starting selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, especially women and people with additional SIADH or sodium-lowering risk factors
edges.mechanism: SSRIs can provoke syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, leading to dilutional hyponatremia. Older age, female sex, low body mass, concurrent diuretics, and acute medical illness can magnify that susceptibility and make the sodium drop clinically important rather than biochemical only.
edges.summary: The overall signal is clearly harmful and strongest soon after treatment initiation. While not every older patient on an SSRI develops clinically significant hyponatremia, the risk is high enough and early enough that sodium monitoring and drug selection deserve more attention in frail older adults.
edges.caveats: The largest modern datasets combine SSRIs with some closely related serotonergic antidepressants or compare classes rather than individual molecules, so class-wide estimates may conceal meaningful drug-to-drug variation. Even so, the direction of risk is consistent enough that this edge should be treated as a real safety concern, not an isolated case-report phenomenon.
